'''''Mesembryanthemum crystallinum''''' (the '''common''', '<nowiki/>'''crystalline'''<nowiki/>' or '<nowiki/>'''crystallinum'''<nowiki/>' '''iceplant''', or simply ''''iceplant'''<nowiki/>') is a [[species]] of [[Annual plant|annual]]/[[perennial]], [[Succulent plant|succulent]] [[flowering plant]] in the ''[[Mesembryanthemum]]'' [[genus]] of the [[Aizoaceae]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]]. 

A true [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean-climate]] grower, this [[Prostrate shrub|prostrate]] [[groundcover]] is [[Native species|native]] to coastal [[North Africa]] and [[Sinai Peninsula|Sinai]], the [[Levant]] and maritime [[Southern Europe]], and several [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] and [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic]] islands, as well. The plant is covered with large, glistening bladder cells, or water vesicles, hence its many common names such as '''crystallinum''' '''iceplant''', '''crystalline iceplant''' or '''iceplant'''.<ref name="grin">{{cite web |title=Taxon: ''Mesembryanthemum crystallinum'' L. |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?24132 |work=Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN) |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service |format= |accessdate=2017-06-22}}</ref>

==Description==

''Mesembryanthemum crystallinum'' grows creeping stems, from {{Convert|20-60|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in length.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/331/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=331–332 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|2-10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long.<ref name=":1" />
It flowers from March to October.<ref name=":1" /> The many-petalled flowers, {{Convert|2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} across,<ref name=":1" /> open in the morning and close at night, and are pollinated by insects.<ref name="water" />

The species is covered with enlarged epidermal cells, called "bladder cells", the main function of which is to reserve water.<ref name=water>{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/cpbr/WfHC/Mesembryanthemum/index.html |title= ''Mesembryanthemum crystallinum'' L. |accessdate=2014-04-14  |work=Water for a Healthy Country |publisher=CSIRO}}</ref>
The plant can be annual, biennial or perennial, but its life cycle is usually completed within several months, depending on environmental conditions.<ref name="water" />

=== Biology ===
The plant usually uses [[C3 carbon fixation]], but when it becomes water- or salt-stressed, it is able to switch to [[Crassulacean acid metabolism]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tallman |first1=Gary |last2=Zhu |first2=Jianxin |last3=Mawson |first3=Bruce T. |last4=Amodeo |first4=Gabriella |last5=Nouhi |first5=Zepedeh |last6=Levy |first6=Kathleen |last7=Zeiger |first7=Eduardo |year=1997 |title=Induction of CAM in ''Mesembryanthemum crystallinum'' Abolishes the Stomatal Response to Blue Light and Light-Dependent Zeaxanthin Formation in Guard Cell Chloroplasts |journal=Plant and Cell Physiology |volume=38 |issue=3 |pages=236–42 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.pcp.a029158}}</ref> Like many salt-tolerant plants, ''M. crystallinum'' accumulates salt throughout its life, in a gradient from the roots to the shoots, with the highest concentration stored in epidermal bladder cells. The salt is released by leaching once the plant dies, resulting in a detrimental osmotic environment preventing the growth of other, non-[[salt-tolerant]] species while allowing ''M. crystallinum'' seeds to germinate.<ref name="water" />

In ''M. crystallinum'', the number of seeds produced depends on whether CAM has been activated (C3 metabolism is more efficient) and the size the plant has grown to in its juvenile growth phase. Older portions of the plant progressively die off and dry out during seed production. The developing seed capsules continue to sequester salt and produce viable seeds. Seeds at the top of the capsule generally germinate immediately on imbibation, while seeds at the base may remain dormant for longer than four weeks.<ref name="water" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Mesembryanthemum crystallinum'' is native to [[Africa]], [[Sinai Peninsula|Sinai]] and southern [[Europe]], and naturalized in the Southwest of [[North America]],<ref name=":1" /> as well as in [[South America]] and [[Australia]].<ref name="grin" /> It is found on a wide range of soil types, from well-drained sandy soils (including sand dunes), to loamy and clay soils. It can tolerate nutritionally poor or saline soils ([[halophile]]), and grows well in disturbed sites such as roadsides, rubbish dumps and homestead yards.<ref name="water" />

==Ecology==
''M. crystallinum'' is listed as an [[invasive species]] in North America, South America, and Australia.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-03-20 |title=Mesembryanthemum crystallinum Profile |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/mesembryanthemum-crystallinum-profile/ |access-date=2022-03-16 |website=California Invasive Plant Council |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Nick |date=2017-04-01 |title=WEED NOTE Mid-West: Ice plant (Mesembryanthemum crystallinum) |url=https://cdn-sharkbaywa.pressidium.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Mesembryanthemum_crystallinum_ice_plant.pdf |access-date=2022-03-16 |website=Shark Bay World Heritage Area |publisher=Astron Environmental Services Pty Ltd.}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Vivrette |first1=Nancy J. |last2=Muller |first2=Cornelius H. |date=June 1977 |title=Mechanism of Invasion and Dominance of Coastal Grassland by Mesembryanthemum crystallinum |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/1942519 |journal=Ecological Monographs |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=301–318 |doi=10.2307/1942519 |jstor=1942519 |issn=0012-9615|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its ability to grow in poor quality or saline soils and preference for disturbed areas are traits shared by many invasive plants which enable them to outcompete [[native species]]. In addition salt sequestration over the plant's lifetime, and the subsequent leaching into the soil upon its death, create an environment in which other plant's seeds struggle to [[Germination|germinate]], allowing for the colonization of new areas with very little competition.<ref name="water" /><ref name=":0" />

The plant is rarely, if ever, grazed upon by domestic stock.<ref name="water" />

==Uses==
[[Image:Yaiza Las Casitas - LZ-702 - Mesembryanthemum crystallinum 02 ies.jpg|thumb|right|200px|A younger plant in Lanzarote]]
The leaves are edible,<ref name="sanderson">{{cite book |last1=Sanderson |first1=Helen |url=https://archive.org/details/culturalhistoryo0000unse_q6u7/page/120/ |title=The Cultural History of Plants |last2=Renfrew |first2=Jane M. |date=2005 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=0415927463 |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |page=120 |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark}}</ref> as with some other members of the family [[Aizoaceae]]. The plant was once promoted in the [[United States]] and [[Europe]] as a vegetable similar to [[spinach]], but failed to gain popularity.<ref name="sanderson" /> In southern Africa, the leaves and stems are gathered from the wild and pickled.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}} In Japan, the plant has become a common vegetable sold in supermarkets after [[Saga University]] succeeded in [[hydroponic]] cultivation of a commercial quantity in 2009; the vegetable goes by the names ice plant (アイスプラント), salt leaf (ソルトリーフ) and barafu (バラフ).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Desaki |first=Yutaro |date=2009-11-28 |title=Universities bringing research to the plate |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2009/11/28/national/universities-bringing-research-to-the-plate/ |access-date=2021-02-21 |website=The Japan Times |language=en-US}}</ref> The seeds are also edible.<ref name="water" />

The crushed leaves can be used as a [[soap substitute]] and have medicinal uses.<ref name="water" /> Ice plants are also used in South Africa as a way of deterring fires, or "firescaping" gardens.<ref name="sanderson" /> It is also cultivated for [[ornamental plant|ornamentation]].<ref name="grin" /> Due to its salt accumulation, ''M. crystallinum'' may be useful for [[bioremediation]].<ref name="water" />
